Mergers and Acquisitions: Types, Process, Swap Ratio and Synergy

Companies combine to grow faster, cut costs or enter new markets. This guide covers the forms of combination, how a deal is done, and how it is valued, with a swap ratio example.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Forms of restructuring

FormMeaning
MergerTwo companies become one, and one usually survives
AmalgamationCompanies combine, often into a new entity
Acquisition or takeoverOne company buys control of another
DemergerA division becomes a separate company
Slump saleA whole business unit is sold for one price
DivestmentA stake or unit is sold
Leveraged buyoutA purchase funded mostly by debt

Types of mergers

  • Horizontal: competitors in the same business combine, gaining scale and market share.
  • Vertical: firms at different stages of the same supply chain combine, such as a manufacturer and its supplier.
  • Conglomerate: unrelated businesses combine, for diversification.
  • Concentric: related businesses with different products combine, sharing customers or technology.

Why companies merge

  • Synergy: the combined value is greater than the sum of the two.
  • Economies of scale and lower costs.
  • New markets, products or technology.
  • Tax benefits, such as carried-forward losses, within the law.
  • Elimination of a competitor, which the Competition Commission of India (CCI) checks.

The process of a deal

  • Strategy and search for targets.
  • Initial valuation and a non-binding offer.
  • Due diligence into finances, legal issues, tax and operations.
  • Negotiation and a final agreement.
  • Approvals from the board, shareholders, the NCLT, CCI and sectoral regulators where required.
  • An open offer if SEBI's takeover rules are triggered: generally on acquiring 25% or more of a listed company.
  • Integration, which is where many deals fail.

Swap ratio: a worked example

In a share-for-share merger, the swap ratio sets how many acquirer shares are given for each target share.

Acquirer's value per share ₹200, target's value per share ₹50. Swap ratio = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25. So 1 acquirer share is issued for every 4 target shares. A holder of 1,000 target shares receives 250 acquirer shares.

In practice, value per share is based on a mix of methods, and independent valuers often give a fairness opinion.

How a target is valued

  • Discounted cash flow: the present value of future free cash flows.
  • Comparable companies: multiples such as EV/EBITDA and P/E.
  • Precedent transactions: prices paid in similar deals.
  • Net asset value: mostly for asset-heavy businesses.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between a merger and an acquisition?

In a merger, two companies combine into one, usually by agreement. In an acquisition, one company buys control of another, which may keep operating separately.

What is synergy?

Extra value from combining: cost savings, more revenue or financial benefits. If two firms worth ₹100 crore and ₹50 crore are worth ₹170 crore together, synergy is ₹20 crore.

Why do many mergers fail to create value?

Often because the acquirer overpays, overestimates synergies, or struggles to integrate people, systems and cultures.
